title: 1000 Layer Networks for Self-Supervised RL: Scaling Depth Can Enable New G

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states 'Increasing model depth improves success rates modestly and occasionally corresponds to emergent behaviors in some humanoid tasks,' yet the body text and Table 1 report gains of up to 42x, 40x, and 600x on humanoid tasks and over 20x on long-horizon maze tasks (Section 4.2: 'over 50× gains in humanoid-based tasks'). Describing these as 'modest' directly contradicts the magnitude of results reported elsewhere in the paper.

Table 1 lists D=4 value as 0.06 ± 0.04 and D=64 value as 40 ± 21, with an 'Imprv.' column of '600×'. The actual ratio 40/0.06 ≈ 667×, not 600×, an inconsistency not seen in other rows (e.g., 11.4→230 correctly rounds to ~20×, 0.97→49 correctly rounds to ~50×).

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 6 caption and Section 4.4 (Scaling the Actor vs. Critic Networks)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The caption claims 'coordinated depth increases resulting in an average 30% improvement over critic-only or actor-only scaling across tasks.' Computing from the reported numbers (e.g., Humanoid: critic-only=680, both=718, ≈5.6% gain; Ant Big Maze: critic-only=462, both=571, ≈23.6% gain; Arm Push Easy: critic-only=817, both=864, ≈5.75% gain) yields an average improvement of roughly 12%, not 30%.

Critic Depth 16 values for Humanoid (15, 17, 20, 22, 25) and Arm Push Easy (170, 195, 210, 230, 250) are drastically lower than both Critic Depth 8 (622-670; 802-860) and Critic Depth 32 (450-480; 800-839), an anomalous non-monotonic dip inconsistent with the surrounding trend and with the Ant Big Maze data in the same figure, which does increase monotonically at depth 16.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4 (Width vs. Depth) and Appendix B.6
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.4 claims 'the parameter count scales linearly with width but quadratically with depth,' but for a stack of dense layers of fixed width W and depth D, parameter count scales as D·W^2 — linear in depth, quadratic in width. This is confirmed by the paper's own numeric example (4 layers × 2048 width ≈ 35M vs 32 layers × 256 width ≈ 2M, consistent with linear-in-depth/quadratic-in-width scaling) and directly contradicted by Appendix B.6, which correctly states FLOPs and memory 'scale quadratically with width but only linearly with depth.'

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2 / Appendix A.1 'Figure 12' vs. Section 4.4 'Figure 12' (Testing the limits of scale)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 12 is captioned in Appendix A.1 as 'Scaled CRL (ours) outperforms baselines CRL (original), SAC, SAC+HER, TD3+HER, GCSL, and GCBC in 8 out of 10 environments,' matching the reference in Section 4.2. However, the same figure number is reused later: 'The results, shown in Figure 12, indicate that performance continues to substantially improve as network depth reaches 256 and 1024 layers...' and the corresponding caption reads 'Figure 12: Testing the limits of scale.' These are two unrelated figures sharing the same number.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3 (Contrastive Reinforcement Learning) vs. Figure 9 and Table of Hyperparameters
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 3 defines the critic as a dot-product similarity: f_{φ,ψ}(s,a,g) = φ(s,a)^T ψ(g). However, Figure 9 visualizes Q-values as Q(s,a,g) = ||φ(s,a) − ψ(g)||_2 (an L2 distance, not a dot product), and the hyperparameter table lists 'energy_function: L2,' contradicting the dot-product formulation stated in the Preliminaries.

Figure 1's caption states critical depths correspond to emergent qualitatively distinct policies, citing '64 on Humanoid U-Maze.' However, Section 4.3 states: 'In the Humanoid U-Maze environment, networks of depth 64 struggle to navigate around the intermediary wall, collapsing on the ground,' and that the qualitatively novel behavior only emerges at depth 256, contradicting the figure caption's claim that 64 is the critical depth for emergent behavior in this task.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.4 'Deep Networks Unlock Batch Size Scaling' and Figure 7
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The subsection header and Figure 7 caption assert 'Deeper networks unlock batch size scaling' and that 'larger networks can effectively leverage batch size scaling to achieve further improvements,' yet the accompanying body text concludes 'Figure 7 shows only marginal or inconsistent improvements from increasing batch size, even for larger depth models... the overall benefit of batch size scaling remains uncertain,' directly contradicting the stronger claim made in the heading and caption.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 3 vs. Table 4 (Humanoid U-Maze wall-clock times)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 3 reports Humanoid U-Maze wall-clock times of 8.72, 11.29, 16.36, 26.48, and 46.74 hours for depths 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 respectively. Table 4, covering the same environment and same depths, reports 3.23, 4.19, 6.07, 9.83, and 17.33 hours — roughly 2.5-3x lower at every depth, with no explanation given for the discrepancy despite purportedly measuring the same experimental setup.

predicted_errors.error_location: Title ('1000 Layer Networks') and Figure 12 caption (Testing the limits of scale)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper's title and abstract emphasize scaling to '1024 layers,' but the caption of the 1024-layer experiment notes: 'we maintained the actor depth at 512 while using 1024-layer networks only for the two critic encoders' due to training instability, meaning no full network (actor+critic) was actually trained at 1024 layers, which overstates the scale implied by the title.
